claims.text: Whiff test: fishy odor before or after 10% KOH is one of the four Amsel criteria; at least three of four needed (key takeaway, whiff section, FAQ)
claims.quote: Clinical diagnosis of BV by Amsel criteria requires at least three of the following four symptoms or signs: ... A fishy odor of vaginal discharge before or after addition of 10% KOH (i.e., the whiff test)

claims.text: Other Amsel criteria: thin homogeneous discharge coating the vaginal walls, pH above 4.5, clue cells
claims.quote: Homogeneous, thin discharge (milklike consistency) that smoothly coats the vaginal walls Clue cells (e.g., vaginal epithelial cells studded with adherent bacteria) on microscopic examination pH of vaginal fluid >4.5

claims.text: Douching: no data support it for treatment or symptom relief; might increase relapse (summary, takeaway, hygiene section, FAQ)
claims.quote: Douching might increase the risk for relapse, and no data support use of douching for treatment or symptom relief.

claims.text: Recommended regimens: metronidazole 500 mg orally twice daily 7 days; metronidazole 0.75% gel one full applicator (5 g) once daily 5 days; clindamycin 2% cream one full applicator (5 g) at bedtime 7 days
claims.quote: Recommended Regimens for Bacterial Vaginosis 500 mg orally 2 times/day for 7 days or one full applicator (5 g) intravaginally, once daily for 5 days or one full applicator (5 g) intravaginally at bedtime for 7 days

claims.text: Alternatives: secnidazole 2 g oral granules single dose, tinidazole, oral clindamycin, clindamycin ovules
claims.quote: Alternative Regimens 300 mg orally 2 times/day for 7 days or 100 mg intravaginally once at bedtime for 3 days* or 2 g oral granules in a single dose or 2 g orally once daily for 2 days

claims.text: Secnidazole is an alternative because of higher cost and lack of long-term outcomes
claims.quote: Secnidazole is listed as an alternative regimen, due to its higher cost and lack of long-term outcomes compared with recommended BV treatments.

claims.text: BV is replacement of lactic acid producing lactobacilli by high concentrations of anaerobes with a polymicrobial biofilm; FAQ: BV involves a biofilm
claims.quote: BV is a vaginal dysbiosis resulting from replacement of normal hydrogen peroxide and lactic-acid–producing species in the vagina with high concentrations of anaerobic bacteria ... A notable feature is the appearance of a polymicrobial biofilm on vaginal epithelial cells

claims.text: BV is the most common cause of vaginal discharge worldwide
claims.quote: BV is a highly prevalent condition and the most common cause of vaginal discharge worldwide

claims.text: Amine odor right after KOH suggests BV or trichomoniasis, so a positive whiff test is not specific to BV
claims.quote: samples that emit an amine odor immediately upon application of KOH suggest BV or trichomoniasis

claims.text: Trichomoniasis can cause a discharge that is diffuse, malodorous or yellow-green, with or without vulvar irritation
claims.quote: women with trichomoniasis sometimes have vaginal discharge, which can be diffuse, malodorous, or yellow-green with or without vulvar irritation

claims.text: CDC recommends testing for trichomoniasis in women seeking care for vaginal discharge
claims.quote: Diagnostic testing for [T. vaginalis] should be performed for women seeking care for vaginal discharge.

claims.text: None of the yeast symptoms is specific; yeast symptoms include itching, soreness
claims.quote: Typical symptoms of VVC include pruritus, vaginal soreness, dyspareunia, external dysuria, and abnormal vaginal discharge. None of these symptoms is specific for VVC.

claims.text: pH paper; elevated pH above 4.5 common with BV or trichomoniasis; pH testing not highly specific
claims.quote: The pH of the vaginal secretions can be measured by pH paper; an elevated pH (i.e., >4.5) is common with BV or trichomoniasis ... Because pH testing is not highly specific

claims.text: Yeast infection associated with a normal pH below 4.5 (text and table)
claims.quote: vaginitis is associated with normal vaginal pH (<4.5).

claims.text: A history alone is not enough for accurate diagnosis of vaginitis and can lead to the wrong medication
claims.quote: Obtaining a medical history alone has been reported to be insufficient for accurate diagnosis of vaginitis and can lead to inappropriate administration of medication

claims.text: BV prevalence increases during menses
claims.quote: In addition, BV prevalence increases during menses

claims.text: Vulvovaginal inflammation without infection can have chemical or allergic causes (cited after the sentence that scented washes, wipes and sprays are not BV treatments)
claims.quote: Presence of objective signs of vulvovaginal inflammation in the absence of vaginal pathogens after laboratory testing indicates the possibility of mechanical, chemical, allergic, or other noninfectious causes

claims.text: People often try OTC products before or alongside a clinician visit
claims.quote: symptomatic women often seek these products before or in addition to an evaluation by a medical provider

claims.text: Treating BV relieves its symptoms
claims.quote: Established benefits of therapy among nonpregnant women are to relieve vaginal symptoms and signs of infection.

claims.text: Retreatment with the same regimen is acceptable after a first recurrence; options for multiple recurrences
claims.quote: retreatment with the same recommended regimen is an acceptable approach for treating persistent or recurrent BV after the first occurrence

claims.text: Twice-weekly metronidazole gel for more than 3 months reduces recurrences; benefit does not persist after stopping
claims.quote: either 0.75% metronidazole gel or 750 mg metronidazole vaginal suppository twice weekly for >3 months has been reported to reduce recurrences, although this benefit does not persist when suppressive therapy is discontinued

claims.text: Boric acid (limited data, multiple recurrences): oral nitroimidazole 7 days, then boric acid 600 mg daily 21 days, then twice-weekly gel 4 to 6 months (section and FAQ)
claims.quote: for women with multiple recurrences, an oral nitroimidazole (metronidazole or tinidazole 500 mg 2 times/day for 7 days), followed by intravaginal boric acid 600 mg daily for 21 days and suppressive 0.75% metronidazole gel twice weekly for 4–6 months

claims.text: FAQ: boric acid is not part of CDC regimens for a first episode (read from its placement only under multiple recurrences)
claims.quote: Limited data indicate that for women with multiple recurrences ... intravaginal boric acid 600 mg daily for 21 days

claims.text: CDC does not recommend routine treatment of sex partners
claims.quote: Therefore, routine treatment of sex partners is not recommended.

claims.text: CDC advises returning for evaluation when symptoms recur
claims.quote: Because persistent or recurrent BV is common, women should be advised to return for evaluation if symptoms recur.

claims.text: Lack of condom use and douching are associated with BV
claims.quote: BV is associated with having multiple male sex partners, female partners, sexual relationships with more than one person, a new sex partner, lack of condom use, douching

claims.text: PID often missed because signs such as abnormal bleeding, pain with sex and vaginal discharge are mild or nonspecific (not-BV section, red flags, FAQ)

claims.text: Pelvic or lower abdominal pain in at-risk women is a reason to consider PID treatment
claims.quote: Presumptive treatment for PID should be initiated for sexually active young women and other women at risk for STIs if they are experiencing pelvic or lower abdominal pain

claims.text: Temperature above 101 F is among findings that support PID diagnosis
claims.quote: Oral temperature >38.3°C (>101°F)

claims.text: Treat all symptomatic BV in pregnancy because of links with preterm birth and other complications
claims.quote: BV treatment is recommended for all symptomatic pregnant women because symptomatic BV has been associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes, including premature rupture of membranes, preterm birth

claims.text: Symptoms during pregnancy are a reason to see a clinician rather than self-treat (inferred from treat-all-symptomatic recommendation)
claims.quote: BV treatment is recommended for all symptomatic pregnant women

claims.text: FAQ: a foul smell can point to other causes such as trichomoniasis
